issues.explanation: 'Noticing Weapons' is a poor fit for the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is evidence of weapon-related assault or generalized violence cues; the rest of the profile centers on interpersonal abuse and nonspecific danger rather than weapon-focused threat monitoring, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma context.

'Inaction Guilt' is clinically questionable in this context because it implies self-blame for not doing more to stop the abuse, which is less coherent with an ongoing coercive partner-abuse formulation than appraisals centered on shame, powerlessness, betrayal, or worthlessness. It is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it stands out as weakly aligned with the trauma narrative and node pattern.

vignette:
Minh is a 51-year-old Vietnamese American man who works as a tax inspector for a regional government office. He was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to his primary care physician of ongoing sleep difficulties, hypervigilance, and intrusive memories connected to a period of sustained physical abuse perpetrated by his former domestic partner, which ended approximately three years ago. His current PCL-5 score of 39 places him in the clinically significant range, and he presents as guarded but cooperative, speaking carefully and with long pauses.

The abuse unfolded over several years in what Minh had understood to be a committed relationship. His former partner's violence was characteristically unpredictable - erupting without warning from ordinary evenings, often when Minh had returned home exhausted after long hours at work. He recalls one night in particular: he had come home fatigued after a difficult audit cycle, sat down at the kitchen table, and within minutes found himself shielding his face from blows. There was no argument, no escalation he could trace. The randomness of it was, in some ways, the most damaging feature - because it meant that any moment of tiredness or discomfort, any situation he could not read in advance, became indistinguishable from the conditions that had preceded violence. He had learned, at a physiological level, that exhaustion and unpredictability were not merely unpleasant states but signals of imminent danger.

In the years since leaving, Minh has found that these same states reliably pull him back. When he feels the particular heaviness of fatigue at the end of a working day - sitting at his desk reviewing returns, or driving home through familiar streets - his body responds as though the threat is present: his heart rate climbs, he finds himself scanning doorways, pressing his back to whatever solid surface is nearest so that the room remains visible ahead of him. He frequently checks over his shoulder when walking between office floors, certain in those moments that someone is close behind him. He knows, intellectually, that nothing is wrong; yet the alarm is total and convincing. These episodes of perceived threat, in turn, are themselves triggering - the physiological arousal and the posture of vigilance recreate something close enough to the original conditions of danger that fragments of memory begin to surface unbidden: a hand raised, the sound of a chair scraping, the particular quality of silence that preceded the worst nights. These fragments arrive suddenly and without coherence, then vanish before he can examine them, leaving him disoriented. There are portions of those years he cannot access at all, no matter how deliberately he tries, which troubles him in its own way.

When the memories do force themselves through, they carry with them a weight of interpretation that has, over time, hardened into conviction. Minh has come to believe that he was fundamentally betrayed - not merely hurt, but deceived at the level of identity, by someone he had trusted completely. From this, a broader and more damaging conclusion has followed: that he is not a person to whom good things happen, that the future holds nothing he can reasonably hope for. He describes himself, haltingly, as feeling like an object in his own life - acted upon, without agency or worth. These appraisals do not remain static; they actively shape his daily experience. Because he believes himself to be without a meaningful future and essentially without personhood, ordinary discomforts and uncertainties feel freighted with confirmation - any unpredictable moment at work, any colleague whose mood he cannot read, registers immediately as potential threat, returning him to the vigilant scanning and the intrusive fragments that characterise his worst days. The cycle is self-sustaining in a way he has begun to recognise but cannot interrupt alone.

Minh has been married for six years to a woman he describes as patient and kind, though he acknowledges that his hypervigilance and emotional withdrawal have placed significant strain on their relationship. His wife recently told him she no longer recognises him at home. It was this - more than the sleeplessness, more than the checking and the scanning - that finally brought him to seek help. What he fears most is that nothing can be different. What he hopes, cautiously, is that he might be wrong about that.
